source.title: George Washington's Rules of Civility
source.attribution: George Washington, George Washington's Rules of Civility, Project Gutenberg, public domain
source.notes: The 110 rules were copied out by the teenage Washington around 1744-45 from an older English version of French Jesuit maxims. This text is the 1890 edition edited, with an introduction and commentary, by Moncure D. Conway (Project Gutenberg #12029). Quotes keep Washington's original spelling; words in square brackets are Conway's restorations of damaged parts of the manuscript. Public domain.

cards.title: Let everything you do in company show respect for the people there
cards.body:
The very first rule sets the tone for all the rest: whatever you do in front of others should carry some sign that you respect them. It is less a rule than a lens. Small actions, like where your eyes go or whether you finish a sentence before turning away, tell people how much they count.

Today the test is often your phone. Checking it mid-conversation, typing through a meeting, or answering a message while someone is speaking all quietly say "you matter less than this." Respect in company is mostly attention, given on purpose.
cards.quote: 1st. Every Action done in Company ought to be with Some Sign of Respect, to those that are Present.
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, put your phone face down and out of reach until it ends.

quiz.question: What does Washington's first rule ask of every action done in company?
options: That it be quick and efficient
That it show some sign of respect to those present
That it impress people of higher rank
That it follow the latest fashion
quiz.explanation: Rule 1 says every action in company should show some sign of respect to those present, which frames all the rules that follow.

cards.title: Don't show friends things that will upset or frighten them
cards.body:
Rule 3 is one line long: show nothing to your friend that may frighten him. The French maxim behind it says nothing that may grieve him. The point is simple consideration. You may find something gripping, gross or shocking, but the other person never agreed to see it.

This fits modern life almost too well. A graphic video in the group chat, a disturbing news clip pushed onto someone's screen, a horror prank on a nervous friend. Before you share, ask whether the other person would choose to see it. A quick "this is upsetting, want to see it?" lets them decide for themselves.
cards.quote: Shew Nothing to your Friend that may affright him.
cards.apply_it: Before forwarding anything graphic or distressing, add a short warning and let the other person choose whether to open it.

quiz.question: What is the courtesy behind Rule 3?
options: Only show friends things you made yourself
Don't spring frightening or upsetting things on a friend
quiz.explanation: Rule 3 warns against showing a friend anything that may frighten him; the French original adds anything that may grieve him.

cards.title: Keep your small noises to yourself in shared spaces
cards.body:
Several of the rules deal with the little sounds and movements we barely notice in ourselves: humming, drumming fingers or feet, loud yawns and sneezes. Rule 4 asks you not to hum or drum in front of others, and Rule 5 says to cough, sneeze or yawn quietly, covering your face and turning aside.

In an open-plan office, a shared flat or a video call, these habits land on everyone around you. A tapping pen, a jiggling leg on an unmuted mic, a speakerphone call on the train. None of it is wicked, it just takes a little of other people's peace without asking.
cards.quote: In the Presence of Others sing not to yourself with a humming Noise, nor Drum, with your Fingers or Feet.
cards.apply_it: Notice one habit you do without thinking (tapping, humming, loud calls) and catch yourself at it in shared spaces this week.

quiz.question: Which pair of habits does Rule 4 ask you to avoid around others?
options: Humming to yourself and drumming with fingers or feet
quiz.explanation: Rule 4 says not to sing to yourself with a humming noise, nor drum with your fingers or feet, in the presence of others.

cards.title: Give people room, and never point at the person you're talking about
cards.body:
Rule 76 bundles two everyday courtesies. Don't point your finger at the person you are talking about, and don't stand too close to the one you are talking to, especially right in their face. Rule 12 adds, with eighteenth-century frankness, that you shouldn't spray anyone by talking too near.

Pointing turns a person into an object of discussion, and everyone in the room feels it. Crowding someone makes them lean back and stop listening. Comfortable distance differs between cultures and people, so watch for the small step backwards that tells you to give more room.
cards.quote: While you are talking, Point not with your Finger at him of Whom you Discourse nor Approach too near him to whom you talk especially to his face
cards.apply_it: In your next few conversations, notice how close you stand. If the other person shifts back, take a half step back too.

quiz.question: According to Rule 76, what two things should you avoid while talking?
options: Pointing at the person you discuss and standing too close to your listener
quiz.explanation: Rule 76 says not to point at the person you are talking about, nor approach too near the one you are talking to.

cards.title: Fix a friend's small embarrassment quietly, and thank whoever fixes yours
cards.body:
Buried in Rule 13 is a gem. If you see something on a companion's clothes, remove it privately. If someone does the same for you, thank them.

The modern versions are endless: spinach in someone's teeth, a label sticking up, toilet paper on a shoe, a typo in a slide just before the client arrives. The kind move is to tell them quietly, not to announce it or let them walk around unaware. And when you are the one being told, the gracious reply is "thank you", not defensiveness. Both halves make it easier for people to look out for each other.
cards.quote: if it be upon the Cloths of your Companions, Put it off privately, and if it be upon your own Cloths return Thanks to him who puts it off
cards.apply_it: Next time you notice a small slip on someone (food in teeth, a typo on their screen), tell them privately and quickly.

quiz.question: What does Rule 13 say to do when someone removes something from your clothes?
options: Tell everyone it wasn't your fault
Return thanks to the person who removed it
quiz.explanation: Rule 13 says to put off something on a companion's clothes privately, and to return thanks when someone does it for you.

cards.title: Don't read your messages in company unless you ask first
cards.body:
Rule 18 opens with advice that could have been written for smartphones: read no letters, books or papers in company, and if you really must, ask leave first. Rule 77 adds: deal with business at a fitting time, and don't whisper in company.

Scrolling a feed or answering a message while with people is the modern letter, and private chats running during a meeting are the modern whisper. Sometimes you genuinely need to check something. Then just say so: "Sorry, I need to answer this, it's about my kid." Asking leave turns a small rudeness into a shared understanding.
cards.quote: Read no Letters, Books, or Papers in Company but when there is a Necessity for the doing of it you must ask leave
cards.apply_it: If you must check your phone with someone, say why first and keep it brief.

quiz.question: What does Rule 18 say to do if you must read something while in company?
options: Read it quickly so nobody notices
Leave the room without a word
quiz.explanation: Rule 18 says to read no letters or papers in company unless necessary, and then you must ask leave.

cards.title: Keep your eyes off other people's screens and private business
cards.body:
The second half of Rule 18 forbids peering at someone else's books or writing, giving opinions on it unasked, or looking over while they write a letter. Rule 81 goes further: don't be curious about other people's affairs, and don't sidle up to those talking privately.

The modern equivalents are reading someone's messages over their shoulder on the bus, glancing at a colleague's inbox, or commenting on a draft nobody asked you to see. Each one shrinks the private space everyone needs. If you are curious, wait to be invited. Most people will share what they want you to know.
cards.quote: Be not Curious to Know the Affairs of Others neither approach to those that Speak in Private
cards.apply_it: When you catch yourself reading someone else's screen, look away, and don't mention what you saw.

quiz.question: Which of these does Rule 81 warn against?
options: Approaching people who are speaking in private
quiz.explanation: Rule 81 says not to be curious about others' affairs or approach those who speak in private.

cards.title: Dress neatly and to fit in, not to be admired
cards.body:
A few rules deal with appearance. Keep clean and brushed, says Rule 51. Rule 52 asks for modest clothes that suit you and the setting rather than ones meant to win admiration. Rule 54 mocks the peacock who keeps looking himself over to see if his shoes and stockings sit well.

The balance still works: care enough to look tidy and right for the occasion, then forget about it. Constantly checking your reflection or your camera preview pulls your attention away from the people in front of you. Neat and suitable, then present.
cards.quote: In your Apparel be Modest and endeavour to accomodate Nature, rather than to procure Admiration keep to the Fashion of your equals
cards.apply_it: Before your next event, choose clothes for the setting, check once in the mirror, then stop checking.

quiz.question: What does Rule 52 say clothing should aim for?
options: Modesty and suiting nature, in line with your equals
quiz.explanation: Rule 52 asks for modest apparel that accommodates nature rather than procures admiration, keeping to the fashion of your equals.

cards.title: Give praise that is honest, not flattering
cards.body:
Rule 17 is blunt: be no flatterer. Rule 67 balances it: don't run other people down, but don't overdo the praise either. The French maxim behind Rule 17 says that whoever tries to win someone over with honeyed words shows he doesn't really respect them, taking them for someone easily tricked.

Flattery cheapens praise. When everything is "amazing", nothing is. Specific, sincere appreciation lands far better: "the way you handled that angry customer was calm and clear" means more than a gush of compliments. It also keeps your word worth something when you really are impressed.
cards.quote: Detract not from others neither be excessive in Commending.
cards.apply_it: Next time you praise someone, name one specific thing they did well instead of a general compliment.

quiz.question: What balance does Rule 67 strike?
options: Don't run others down, and don't overdo praise either
quiz.explanation: Rule 67 says detract not from others, neither be excessive in commending.

cards.title: Only joke when the room is in the mood, and never at someone's misfortune
cards.body:
Several rules shape good humour. Rule 64 says not to crack jokes where nobody is in the mood for fun, not to laugh loudly without reason, and never to mock someone's misfortune even when it seems to invite it. Rule 47 adds: no biting jokes, nothing flippant about serious matters, and don't laugh at your own wit. Rule 17 warns against teasing someone who doesn't enjoy it.

Humour connects people when everyone is in on it. It wounds when it comes at the wrong time or at someone's expense. Look at the faces around you before the punchline.
cards.quote: Break not a Jest where none take pleasure in mirth Laugh not aloud, nor at all without Occasion, deride no man's Misfortune, tho' there seem to be Some cause
cards.apply_it: Before your next joke in a group, glance around: is everyone in a light mood, and is anyone the target?

quiz.question: According to Rule 64, when should you not break a jest?
options: Where nobody takes pleasure in mirth
quiz.explanation: Rule 64 says break not a jest where none take pleasure in mirth, and deride no one's misfortune.

cards.title: "Just joking" doesn't make hurtful words harmless
cards.body:
Rule 65 closes a loophole people still use: speak no injurious words, whether in jest or in earnest, and scoff at no one even if they give you an opening. Rule 49 adds no reproachful language, no cursing, no reviling.

Online, the line between joke and insult blurs fast. A mocking reply, a meme at someone's expense, a "lol, relax" after a cutting remark. The person on the receiving end feels the words, not your intention. If a remark would hurt said seriously, wrapping it in a joke doesn't change much.
cards.quote: Speak not injurious Words neither in Jest nor Earnest Scoff at none although they give Occasion
cards.apply_it: Before posting a jokey reply, ask: would this still be fine if they read it as serious?

quiz.question: What does Rule 65 say about hurtful words spoken in jest?
options: Avoid them in jest as well as in earnest
They are fine if you smile
They are acceptable if the other person started it
quiz.explanation: Rule 65 says speak not injurious words neither in jest nor earnest, and scoff at none although they give occasion.

cards.title: Don't stare at, or ask about, someone's scars and differences
cards.body:
Rule 21 says never to reproach anyone for natural infirmities, or enjoy reminding them of them. Rule 71 adds: don't gaze at the marks or blemishes of others, and don't ask how they came by them.

People with a scar, a stammer, a birthmark, a missing limb or a visible condition are asked about it constantly, often by strangers. Each question, however curious or kindly meant, makes them explain their body again. Let people share their story if and when they want to. Until then, treat the difference as you would anything else that is none of your business.
cards.quote: Gaze not at the marks or blemishes of Others and ask not how they came.
cards.apply_it: If you notice something unusual about someone's body, resist asking. Talk to them about what they choose to bring up.

quiz.question: What does Rule 71 advise about others' marks or blemishes?
options: Point them out so the person knows
Don't gaze at them or ask how they came
quiz.explanation: Rule 71 says gaze not at the marks or blemishes of others and ask not how they came.

cards.title: Don't show glee at anyone's misfortune, even an enemy's
cards.body:
Rule 22 asks a lot: don't look glad at another person's misfortune, even if he is your enemy. Rule 23 is honest about human nature. When you see wrongdoing punished you may feel inwardly satisfied, but always show pity to the person suffering.

Gloating feels good for a moment, but it makes you smaller and hardens the people watching. When a rival fails, a critic is embarrassed or someone you dislike gets their comeuppance online, the dignified move is restraint. You don't have to pretend to be sad, just don't celebrate in public.
cards.quote: Shew not yourself glad at the Misfortune of another though he were your enemy
cards.apply_it: Next time a rival stumbles, notice any flicker of pleasure, then let it pass without comment or a reaction emoji.

quiz.question: What does Rule 22 say about an enemy's misfortune?
options: Do not show yourself glad at it
quiz.explanation: Rule 22: show not yourself glad at the misfortune of another, though he were your enemy.

cards.title: The more power you hold, the more courtesy you owe
cards.body:
Many of the rules deal with rank, but they keep insisting that courtesy flows downward too. Rule 28 says stand up when someone comes to speak to you, even if they are below you. Rule 36 says those of high degree should treat others with affability and courtesy, without arrogance.

In any workplace, people watch how a senior person treats the receptionist, the intern, the cleaner, the waiter. A boss who greets everyone warmly and gives full attention to a junior colleague builds trust that no title can. Rank earns you a seat at the table, not the right to be curt.
cards.quote: those of high Degree ought to treat them with affibility & Courtesie, without Arrogancy
cards.apply_it: This week, give the same full attention and greeting to the most junior person you meet as to the most senior.

quiz.question: According to Rule 36, how should people of high degree treat those below them?
options: With affability and courtesy, without arrogance
quiz.explanation: Rule 36 says those of high degree ought to treat others with affability and courtesy, without arrogance.

cards.title: Be brief, especially with busy people
cards.body:
Rule 35 is a model of its own advice: let your talk with people of business be short and comprehensive. Rule 88 adds: don't be tedious, don't wander into digressions, and don't keep repeating yourself. Rule 80 says don't go on, in talk or reading aloud, unless the company is clearly enjoying it.

The modern test is the email, the voice note and the meeting update. Lead with the point, cover what the person needs, and stop. Being short is a kindness to busy people, and "comprehensive" means short without leaving out what matters.
cards.quote: Let your Discourse with Men of Business be Short and Comprehensive.
cards.apply_it: Rewrite your next work email so the request is in the first line, then cut anything the reader doesn't need.

quiz.question: What two qualities does Rule 35 want in business talk?
quiz.explanation: Rule 35: let your discourse with men of business be short and comprehensive.

cards.title: Don't lecture people on their own profession
cards.body:
Rule 41 warns against teaching your equal in the very art he practises, because it smacks of arrogance. It is a simple, timeless form of humility.

Most of us have watched it happen: explaining medicine to a nurse, cooking to a chef, code to a developer, or someone's own field to them because we read an article. Even when you know something useful, the respectful move is to ask rather than instruct. "What's your take on this?" invites their expertise, where unasked teaching dismisses it.
cards.quote: Undertake not to teach your equal in the art himself Professes; it flavours of arrogancy.
cards.apply_it: When talking with someone about their field, ask one question before offering any opinion.

quiz.question: Why does Rule 41 say not to teach an equal in his own profession?
quiz.explanation: Rule 41 says undertaking to teach your equal in the art he professes flavours of arrogancy.

cards.title: Match the mood: no celebrating beside the suffering, no gloom at the party
cards.body:
Rule 43 says not to show joy in front of someone sick or in pain, because the contrast deepens their misery. Rule 62 is its mirror: don't bring up gloomy things like death and wounds at a time of celebration or at the table, and if others do, change the subject if you can.

Both rules ask you to notice the emotional weather before you speak. Bubbling about your holiday to a friend in hospital, or diving into grim news at a birthday dinner, ignores where others are. Tact is reading the room and meeting it.
cards.quote: Do not express Joy before one sick or in pain for that contrary Passion will aggravate his Misery
cards.apply_it: Before sharing good news, check how the other person is doing first, and let their answer shape what you say.

quiz.question: Why does Rule 43 advise against showing joy before someone in pain?
options: The contrast will aggravate their misery
quiz.explanation: Rule 43: do not express joy before one sick or in pain, for that contrary passion will aggravate his misery.

cards.title: When someone did their best and it still failed, don't blame them
cards.body:
Rule 44 is one of the kindest in the collection: when a person does all they can and it still doesn't work out, don't blame them.

In teams this separates effort from outcome. Projects fail for many reasons, and someone who gave everything and still fell short needs support, not a lecture. Blaming them teaches people to hide problems or stop trying. A better question is what got in the way, and what you can change together next time. It applies at home too, with children, partners and yourself.
cards.quote: When a man does all he can though it Succeeds not well blame not him that did it.
cards.apply_it: Next time something fails, ask "what got in the way?" before asking "whose fault is it?"

quiz.question: What does Rule 44 say about someone who did all they could but failed?
options: Give the task to someone else
quiz.explanation: Rule 44: when a man does all he can though it succeeds not well, blame not him that did it.

cards.title: Correct people privately, at the right time, and without anger
cards.body:
Rule 45 is a short course in giving criticism. Before you advise or correct someone, think about whether to do it in public or in private, now or later, and in what words. And when you do it, show no anger: do it with sweetness and mildness.

Most feedback goes wrong on exactly these points. It is given in front of others, in the heat of the moment, or in a sharp tone. A quiet word afterwards, in calm language, lets the person hear the message instead of defending themselves. The aim is to help them improve, not to win.
cards.quote: in reproving Shew no signs of Cholar but do it with all Sweetness and Mildness
cards.apply_it: Before giving someone critical feedback, decide where, when and how, then wait until you are calm.

quiz.question: Which of these does Rule 45 ask you to consider before correcting someone?
options: Whether to do it in public or in private, and when
How to make an example of them
How to show your anger clearly
quiz.explanation: Rule 45 asks you to consider public or private, now or later, and what words, and to reprove with sweetness and mildness.

cards.title: Take criticism graciously, then clear the record calmly later
cards.body:
Rule 46 handles the other side of feedback. Accept all correction thankfully, whenever and wherever it is given. If you weren't actually at fault, find a suitable time and place afterwards to let the person know.

This is a mature pattern. Arguing back on the spot usually turns feedback into a fight. Saying "thanks, I'll think about it" keeps things calm and lets you check whether they have a point. If they don't, a quiet conversation later sets things straight without anyone losing face. Conway notes that the copy Washington wrote leaves out the original's advice to accept reproof all the more from those you depend on.
cards.quote: Take all Admonitions thankfully in what Time or Place Soever given but afterwards not being culpable take a Time or Place Convenient to let him know it that gave them.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're criticised, reply only "thanks, let me think about that", and decide later whether to respond.

quiz.question: According to Rule 46, what should you do if you were criticised but weren't at fault?
options: Ignore the person from then on
Accept it thankfully, then explain later at a convenient time
quiz.explanation: Rule 46 says take admonitions thankfully, then if not culpable, choose a convenient time and place to let the person know.

cards.title: Your example teaches more than your instructions
cards.body:
Rule 48 says that when you correct someone, make sure you aren't guilty of the same thing, because example is more powerful than precept. Rule 59 adds that you should never say or do anything improper in front of those who look up to you.

Parents, managers, coaches and teachers all learn this the hard way. Asking people to be on time while arriving late, or to stay calm while snapping at them, cancels the message. People copy what you do far more than what you say. If you want a behaviour from others, practise it visibly first.
cards.quote: Wherein wherein you reprove Another be unblameable yourself; for example is is more prevalent than Precepts
cards.apply_it: Pick one thing you often ask of others (punctuality, tidiness, patience) and model it carefully this week.

quiz.question: Why does Rule 48 say you should be blameless before reproving others?
options: Because example is more powerful than precepts
quiz.explanation: Rule 48: wherein you reprove another be unblameable yourself, for example is more prevalent than precepts.

cards.title: Don't pass on news or rumours you haven't checked
cards.body:
Rule 79 says don't be quick to share news if you don't know it is true. Rule 50 adds: don't be quick to believe stories that are spreading to someone's discredit.

In the 1740s rumours moved at walking pace. Today a screenshot can reach thousands in minutes, and a false story about a person can follow them for years. The old advice still holds. Before you forward, ask where it came from and whether it is true. When the story makes someone look bad, slow down even more. Not sharing is always an option.
cards.quote: Be not apt to relate News if you know not the truth thereof.
cards.apply_it: Before sharing your next piece of news or gossip, take a minute to check the source, or don't share it.

quiz.question: What does Rule 79 warn against?
options: Relating news when you don't know whether it's true
quiz.explanation: Rule 79: be not apt to relate news if you know not the truth thereof.

cards.title: Don't press friends for secrets, and keep the ones you're given
cards.body:
Rule 60 asks you not to push a friend to reveal a secret. Rule 79 ends with a short command: a secret, discover not. Rule 71 adds that what you say privately to a friend should not be repeated in front of others.

Trust grows when people feel safe choosing what to share. Pushing for details ("come on, you can tell me") puts them in a bind, and passing on what they told you, even as "don't tell anyone, but...", breaks something hard to repair. Let friends set the pace, and keep their confidences.
cards.quote: Be not immodest in urging your Friends to Discover a Secret
cards.apply_it: If a friend hesitates to tell you something, say "no pressure" and mean it.

quiz.question: What does Rule 60 advise about friends' secrets?
options: Don't be immodest in urging them to reveal a secret
Share them with close family only
quiz.explanation: Rule 60: be not immodest in urging your friends to discover a secret.

cards.title: Choose good company, and know that being alone beats bad company
cards.body:
Rule 56 is about the people you spend time with: keep company with people of good character if you care about your own reputation, because it is better to be alone than in bad company.

The people around us shape our habits, our standards and how others see us. If a group pulls you toward things you aren't proud of, or regularly leaves you feeling worse, the rule gives you permission to step back. A quiet evening alone is not a failure. It may be the healthier choice while you look for people who bring out your best.
cards.quote: Associate yourself with Men of good Quality if you Esteem your own Reputation; for 'tis better to be alone than in bad Company.
cards.apply_it: Think of the five people you spend most time with. Who brings out your best? Plan time with one of them this week.

quiz.question: What does Rule 56 say is better than bad company?
quiz.explanation: Rule 56: 'tis better to be alone than in bad company.

cards.title: Keep malice out of your talk, and let reason steer your temper
cards.body:
Rule 58 asks for conversation free of malice and envy, calling that the sign of a good and teachable nature, and adds that in anything that stirs your passions, let reason govern. Rule 83 says to state your case without heat and with discretion, however lowly the person in front of you.

Strong feelings are normal. The skill is not to let them drive your words. When you notice anger or envy rising, slow down, breathe, and ask what you actually want from the conversation. A calm sentence almost always gets further than a heated one.
cards.quote: let your conversation be without malice or envy, for 'tis a sign of a tractable and commendable nature: & in all causes of passion admit reason to govern
cards.apply_it: When you feel heat rising in a conversation, pause for one breath and ask: what outcome do I actually want?

quiz.question: According to Rule 58, what should govern in all causes of passion?
quiz.explanation: Rule 58 says in all causes of passion admit reason to govern.

cards.title: Fit your topic and language to the people you're talking with
cards.body:
Rule 61 says don't bring trivial chatter to serious, learned people, or hard and abstruse subjects to those who don't know them, or tall tales to anyone. It also says don't stuff your talk with quotations and maxims. Rule 72 adds: speak a language the whole company understands.

Today that covers jargon, in-jokes and acronyms that shut people out, lecturing friends about your niche, or dropping famous quotes to sound clever. Good conversation meets people where they are. If someone looks lost, change your words, not your listener.
cards.quote: Utter not base and frivilous things amongst grave and Learn'd Men nor very Difficult Questions or Subjects, among the Ignorant or things hard to be believed
cards.apply_it: In your next group conversation, swap one piece of jargon or an in-joke for plain words everyone understands.

quiz.question: What does Rule 61 advise about choosing subjects?
options: Always discuss difficult topics to impress
Suit your subject to your listeners
quiz.explanation: Rule 61 says not to bring frivolous things to grave men, nor very difficult subjects to those unfamiliar with them.

cards.title: Don't boast, but don't put yourself down either
cards.body:
Rule 63 strikes a careful balance. Don't make much of your achievements, rare qualities, riches, titles, virtue or family. But, in the words Conway restored from the damaged manuscript, you need not speak meanly of yourself either.

Boasting pushes people away, yet constant self-deprecation is not humility. It can invite pity or make others reassure you. The healthy middle is plain honesty: let your work speak, accept compliments with a simple "thank you", and describe yourself accurately, neither inflated nor shrunk.
cards.quote: A Man ought not to value himself of his Atchievements or rare Qua[lities, his Riches, Tit]les Virtue or Kindred[; but he need not speak meanly of himself.]
cards.apply_it: Next time you're complimented, say "thank you" and stop, without boasting or brushing it off.

quiz.question: What balance does Rule 63 strike?
options: Boast a little so people notice you
Don't vaunt your achievements, but don't speak meanly of yourself
quiz.explanation: Rule 63: don't value yourself for your achievements or rank, but you need not speak meanly of yourself.

cards.title: Be the first to say hello
cards.body:
Rule 66 asks you not to be pushy, but friendly and courteous: be the first to greet, to listen and to answer, and don't sit lost in thought when it is time to talk.

Many people wait for others to make the first move, then feel left out. Greeting first, whether that's saying good morning to the team, waving to a neighbour or saying hi at a party, costs nothing and changes the feel of a place. Listening and answering promptly, rather than leaving messages hanging, is the same warmth in a different form.
cards.quote: Be not forward but friendly and Courteous; the first to Salute hear and answer & be not Pensive when it's a time to converse.
cards.apply_it: Tomorrow, greet three people before they greet you.

quiz.question: What does Rule 66 ask you to be first to do?
quiz.explanation: Rule 66: be friendly and courteous, the first to salute, hear and answer.

cards.title: Don't give advice unless you're asked, and keep it brief when you are
cards.body:
Rule 68 pairs two pieces of social sense. Don't go where you aren't sure you'll be welcome, and don't give advice without being asked. When advice is wanted, give it briefly.

Unasked advice, however well meant, often lands as judgement. Someone sharing a problem may want to be heard, not fixed. A good habit is to ask: "Do you want ideas, or do you just want to vent?" If they do want advice, offer a few clear thoughts, not a lecture.
cards.quote: Give not Advice whth being Ask'd & when desired do it briefly
cards.apply_it: Next time someone tells you a problem, ask whether they want advice before offering any.

quiz.question: What does Rule 68 say about giving advice?
options: Give it whenever you see a problem
Don't give it unasked, and when asked keep it brief
Give it at length so nothing is missed
quiz.explanation: Rule 68: give not advice without being asked, and when desired, do it briefly.

cards.title: In a disagreement, care more about hearing everyone than winning
cards.body:
Rule 86 says don't be so eager to win an argument that you stop others giving their opinion, and accept the judgement of the majority, especially if they are the ones deciding. Rule 87 adds: don't contradict everything others say. Rule 69 says not to take sides in other people's quarrels unless you must, and not to be stubborn about your own opinion.

In meetings, family debates and comment threads, the urge to win can drown out every other voice. Let each person finish, accept the group's decision on things that matter little, and save your pushback for what really counts.
cards.quote: In Disputes, be not so Desirous to Overcome as not to give Liberty to each one to deliver his Opinion
cards.apply_it: In your next disagreement, make sure everyone has spoken before you make your case a second time.

quiz.question: What does Rule 86 warn against in disputes?
options: Being so eager to win that others can't give their opinion
quiz.explanation: Rule 86: in disputes, be not so desirous to overcome as not to give liberty to each one to deliver his opinion.

cards.title: Think before you speak, then speak clearly
cards.body:
Rule 73 is one of the best known: think before you speak. It continues with delivery: don't mumble or rush your words, but bring them out in order and distinctly.

Both halves still matter. A pause before you answer can save a careless remark you'd regret, especially when emotions run high or a message is going to many people. And clear, unhurried speech makes people trust what you say. On calls and in presentations, slowing down slightly almost always helps listeners.
cards.quote: Think before you Speak pronounce not imperfectly nor bring out your Words too hastily but orderly and Distinctly
cards.apply_it: In your next important conversation, pause for a breath before answering any question.

quiz.question: Besides thinking first, what does Rule 73 ask of your speech?
options: That words come out orderly and distinctly, not too hastily
quiz.explanation: Rule 73: think before you speak, and bring out your words orderly and distinctly, not too hastily.

cards.title: Let people finish: don't interrupt, prompt or answer too soon
cards.body:
Rule 74 is a complete guide to listening. When someone else speaks, pay attention and don't distract the audience. If they hesitate, don't jump in to finish their words unless they want help. Don't interrupt, and don't answer until they are done.

Finishing people's sentences feels helpful but often guesses wrong and takes the floor from them. Interrupting, even with agreement, tells them their thought matters less than yours. Waiting until someone has truly finished, then answering, is simple and rare, and people notice it.
cards.quote: When Another Speaks be attentive your Self and disturb not the Audience if any hesitate in his Words help him not nor Prompt him without desired, Interrupt him not, nor Answer him till his Speech be ended
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, count to two after the other person stops before you start talking.

quiz.question: What does Rule 74 say to do if a speaker hesitates over a word?
options: Don't help or prompt them unless they want it
quiz.explanation: Rule 74: if any hesitate in his words, help him not nor prompt him without desired.

cards.title: Arriving late? Don't derail; and when someone joins, bring them up to speed
cards.body:
Rule 75 covers two sides of joining a conversation. If you arrive in the middle, don't ask what it's all about; if people stop because of you, ask them to carry on. And if someone important comes in while you are talking, it is gracious to recap what was said.

This is meeting etiquette today. Joining a call late, don't make everyone start over; catch up quietly or ask afterwards. When you are running the meeting and someone joins late, a ten-second summary helps them contribute without stopping the flow.
cards.quote: If a Person of Quality comes in while your Conversing its handsome to Repeat what was said before
cards.apply_it: When someone joins your next meeting late, give a one-sentence recap so they can follow.

quiz.question: According to Rule 75, what should you do if people stop talking because you arrived?
options: Ask what they were talking about
quiz.explanation: Rule 75 says not to ask what the talk is about, but if there is a stop because of your arrival, request the speaker to proceed.

cards.title: When someone is praised, let them have their moment
cards.body:
Rule 78 says make no comparisons, and if someone in the company is praised for a fine act, don't immediately praise someone else for the same thing.

It's a common reflex. A colleague is thanked for a great presentation and someone says, "Yes, and Sam's last week was excellent too." Or a friend shares an achievement and we mention our own. It may be meant kindly, but it shifts the spotlight. Recognition shared too quickly shrinks. Let the person enjoy it, and save other praise for its own moment.
cards.quote: Make no Comparisons and if any of the Company be Commended for any brave act of Virtue, commend not another for the Same
cards.apply_it: Next time someone is praised, add your own congratulations to them alone, without bringing up anyone else.

quiz.question: What does Rule 78 advise when someone is commended?
options: Mention someone who did it better
Don't commend another for the same thing
quiz.explanation: Rule 78: if any of the company be commended for a brave act, commend not another for the same.

cards.title: Only promise what you can deliver, then deliver it
cards.body:
Rule 82 is short and demanding: don't take on what you can't do, and be careful to keep your promise.

Much unreliability starts with an easy "yes" to a deadline we can't meet, a favour we haven't time for, a "let's catch up soon" we never act on. Each broken promise costs some trust. It's better to say "I can do this part by Friday" than to promise everything and deliver late. Fewer, smaller commitments that you actually keep make you someone people can count on.
cards.quote: Undertake not what you cannot Perform but be Carefull to keep your Promise
cards.apply_it: Before your next "yes", check your calendar. If you can't fully deliver, offer a smaller promise you can keep.

quiz.question: What two things does Rule 82 ask?
options: Don't undertake what you can't perform, and keep your promises
quiz.explanation: Rule 82: undertake not what you cannot perform, but be careful to keep your promise.

cards.title: Don't speak ill of people who aren't there to answer
cards.body:
Rule 89 is one line with a reason attached: speak no evil of the absent, for it is unjust. They can't explain, correct or defend themselves.

Gossip bonds people for a moment, but everyone listening learns that you talk about people behind their backs, and wonders what you say about them. In group chats and office corners, the fair move is to raise concerns with the person directly, or to say nothing. If others start running someone down, a simple "maybe we should ask them" can turn the talk.
cards.quote: Speak not Evil of the absent for it is unjust
cards.apply_it: The next time a conversation turns to criticising someone absent, change the subject or suggest talking to them directly.

quiz.question: Why does Rule 89 say not to speak evil of the absent?
quiz.explanation: Rule 89: speak not evil of the absent, for it is unjust.

cards.title: You can say no, correct or even scold someone kindly
cards.body:
Conway ends his introduction with a passage from Obadiah Walker's book on education, one of the sources behind the rules. It calls civility and affability the greatest magnets in the world, and says affability belongs not only in small talk but in every situation.

The striking claim is that even hard messages can be delivered pleasantly. You can refuse a request, give critical feedback or set a firm boundary with good words. Tone and word choice decide whether people hear you or simply react. Harsh content doesn't need harsh delivery.
cards.quote: A man may deny a request, chide, reprehend, command &c. _affably_, with good words, nor is there anything so harsh which may not be inoffensively represented.
cards.apply_it: Next time you have to say no, start by saying something genuinely warm, then give the no clearly.

quiz.question: What does the Walker passage quoted by Conway say about harsh messages?
options: They must be delivered harshly to be taken seriously
Almost anything harsh can be said inoffensively, with good words
quiz.explanation: It says a man may deny, chide or command affably, and nothing is so harsh it can't be represented inoffensively.

cards.title: Bring good humour to the table, whatever happens
cards.body:
Rule 105 says don't get angry at table, whatever happens. Even if you have reason, don't show it; put on a cheerful face, especially if there are guests, because good humour turns a single dish into a feast. Rule 91 adds don't find fault with the food, and Rule 107 says listen when others talk and don't speak with your mouth full.

Shared meals are among the best moments for connection, and they spoil easily. Arguments, complaints about the cooking or bad moods at dinner leave everyone tasting the tension. Save the hard conversation for after, and bring warmth to the table.
cards.quote: good Humour makes one Dish of Meat a Feast
cards.locator: Chapter viii. 3. Ne prenez pas vostre repas en gourmand ¶54
cards.apply_it: At your next shared meal, leave any complaint or argument until afterwards and focus on the people at the table.

quiz.question: According to Rule 105, what turns one dish into a feast?
quiz.explanation: Rule 105: put on a cheerful countenance, for good humour makes one dish of meat a feast.

cards.title: If you set the pace, set it so the slowest can keep up
cards.body:
Rule 104 describes table manners for the most important person present: they unfold their napkin and begin first, but should start promptly and eat in a way that gives the slowest person time to finish.

The principle reaches well beyond dinner. Whoever leads sets the tempo for everyone else. A manager who rushes through a meeting, or a group leader who strides ahead on a hike, leaves people behind. Moving at a pace that lets the slowest keep up, without dawdling, is a quiet act of leadership.
cards.quote: he ought to begin in time & to Dispatch with Dexterity that y'e Slowest may have time allowed him
cards.locator: Chapter viii. 3. Ne prenez pas vostre repas en gourmand ¶49
cards.apply_it: In the next thing you lead, check in with the person who seems furthest behind before moving on.

quiz.question: According to Rule 104, how should the chief person at table eat?
options: Starting promptly, so the slowest has time allowed
quiz.explanation: Rule 104 says the chief person should begin in time and dispatch with dexterity, that the slowest may have time allowed him.

cards.title: Tend your conscience like a small flame
cards.body:
The last of the 110 rules moves from manners to the inner life: work to keep alive in your heart that little spark of celestial fire called conscience.

It's a fitting end. All the earlier rules about listening, praise, promises and courtesy grow from that inner sense of right and wrong. A spark can be fanned or smothered. Small compromises, ignored once, get easier to ignore again, while honest reflection keeps the flame alive. Conway believed the humility and self-discipline under these rules helped shape the man Washington became.
cards.quote: Labour to keep alive in your Breast that Little Spark of Celestial fire called Conscience.
cards.locator: Chapter viii. 3. Ne prenez pas vostre repas en gourmand ¶71
cards.apply_it: Tonight, ask yourself: was there a moment today my conscience spoke and I ignored it?

quiz.question: How does Rule 110 describe conscience?
options: A little spark of celestial fire
quiz.explanation: Rule 110: labour to keep alive in your breast that little spark of celestial fire called conscience.
